Hatchlings of Lacerta agilis boemica emerge from their incubating eggs with a snout-vent length of 3.1 cm [Lb = 3.1 cm], a size that allows them to begin active foraging almost immediately after shell pipping. This modest neonatal dimension is typical for lacertids of this lineage and is closely linked to the energetic constraints of yolk-dependent embryonic development within the parchment-shelled egg. Under controlled thermal conditions maintained at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the incubation period required for complete development of the embryo lasts 56 days [ab = 56 days], a duration that aligns well with the seven to ten week range reported for other temperate-zone Lacerta species. The relatively protracted incubation is likely an adaptation to cooler montane environments, where slower metabolic rates prolong endogenous yolk utilization. Once the clutch hatches in late summer, the young must feed actively to accumulate sufficient lipid stores before their first winter dormancy. The size of these neonates is a critical determinant of early survival, as larger hatchlings typically enjoy higher rates of overwintering success.

Growing juveniles undergo rapid somatic expansion, and field surveys indicate that the ultimate snout-vent length attained by fully mature individuals approaches 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters] in most populations of this subspecies. This adult size is comparatively moderate among European lacertids and reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes early maturation over extreme longevity. Male Sand lizards in the eastern range often reach this adult dimension by their second active season, while females may continue to grow more slowly after reaching sexual maturity. Reaching this final body size is associated with the cessation of significant vertebral growth, though some individuals may add a few millimeters in especially productive years. The relationship between ultimate SVL and habitat productivity is evident, as lizards from more arid steppe sites tend to be slightly smaller on average. In concert with body mass, this length measurement provides a reliable index of individual condition and is routinely recorded during mark-recapture studies aimed at tracking population health across the species' fragmented range.

The maximum adult wet weight recorded for Lacerta agilis boemica under optimal conditions reaches 12 grams [Wwi = 12 grams], a value that is typical for a lacertid of this ultimate body length. Gravid females in particular may approach this upper limit, as they carry several developing embryonated eggs within their body cavity, each rich in yolk and substantial enough to be externally visible. This mass represents a significant energetic investment for a relatively small reptile, and it is achieved only by individuals that have successfully accumulated sufficient fat reserves during the active season. Body condition fluctuates markedly across the annual cycle, with peak weights observed shortly before oviposition in late spring and minimal weights recorded after emergence from hibernation. Comparisons with related Lacerta agilis subspecies suggest that the boemica lineage may be slightly heavier at a given SVL, possibly reflecting adaptation to the cooler, more continental climate of its eastern range. The sustained ability to reach this adult mass is a prerequisite for successful reproduction.

Reproductive output in this subspecies is strongly influenced by thermal environment. When maintained at a constant 22 °C [T = 22 °C], females achieve their maximum reproductive rate, producing between 7 and 15 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 7 and 15 eggs per clutch] and laying approximately 1.2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.2 clutches per year]. This peak fecundity is realized over a relatively narrow temperature window, as values decline sharply at both lower and higher ambient conditions. The initiation of reproductive activity is tightly synchronized with spring warming, and first clutches are typically deposited in late May. This constrained reproductive schedule reflects the short active season available in the northern and eastern portions of the subspecies' distribution. The combination of moderate clutch size and limited annual frequency is a common pattern among temperate lacertids facing pronounced seasonal constraints.

Under a sustained thermal regime of 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C], Sand lizards of this subspecies reach sexual maturity at approximately 22.5 months after hatching [tp = approximately 22.5 months after hatching], an age that corresponds to the second or third active summer season for most individuals. This timing represents a trade-off between rapid early growth and the need to accumulate sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and nesting. At this same temperature, the maximum documented lifespan recorded in seminatural enclosures reaches about 7.5 years [am = about 7.5 years], though most free-living individuals likely survive for a shorter interval due to predation and environmental stress. The long potential lifespan relative to body size is a notable feature of this lineage.
